Kerc
KERTS
n. (the Transylvanian Cistercian abbey of about 1202, dissolved in 1474 and since Lutheran)
Hungarian Kerc, Romanian Carta, German Kerz, from a local place-name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Kerc on the Olt in Transylvania was founded about 1202 and settled from Igris, the southernmost Cistercian house in the kingdom of Hungary, planted among the Transylvanian Saxons. It was repeatedly raided, and in 1474 Matthias Corvinus dissolved it outright and gave its estates to the provost of Sibiu, the community having dwindled to almost nothing. The Saxon villagers kept the choir of the abbey church as their parish church; they accepted the Reformation in the sixteenth century, and it is a Lutheran parish church still, with the nave standing roofless beside it. The dictionary records Kerc because the transfer was from an order to a congregation, which is the right direction. A flock is committed to overseers and the price of it is named, “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28), and the manner required of those overseers excludes both compulsion and profit, “not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). The pastors God promises are competent to teach, “which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15), and the one qualification that cannot be waived is possession of a message received, “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a parish as the precinct of a church; an overseer as one who superintends; a pastor as a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church; lucre as gain in money; and a flock as a company of beasts, also a Christian congregation.

expand to see more

PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.

OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a bishop; one who has the charge of a church.

PASTOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.

LUCRE, n. Gain in money or goods; profit; usually in an ill sense, or with the sense of something base.

FLOCK, n. A company or collection of sheep or other small animals; a Christian church or congregation.

Key Scripture

Act 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

1Pe 5:2 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;"

Jer 3:15 — "And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding."

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

Modern Corruption

Transylvania's Cistercian abbey of about 1202, dissolved 1474, its choir kept as a Saxon parish church and Lutheran since the Reformation.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a church belongs to a congregation under pastors rather than to an order under an abbot. Kerc's choir passed to the Saxon villagers and is theirs still, and the apostolic charge over such a people names what they cost, “which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).

The live temptation is an oversight exercised for the overseer's benefit, which is how the abbey emptied in the first place. Peter forbids both the coercion and the profit motive, “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2); the pastors God promises are men who can actually teach, “And I will give you pastors according to mine heart” (Jer 3:15); and the irreducible qualification is a received message held fast, “that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek episkopos (G1985), an overseer; Greek poimaino (G4165), to tend as a shepherd; Hebrew raah (H7462), to feed; Greek antechomai (G0472), to hold fast.

expand to see more

Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer, a bishop; “the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers”, Acts 20:28.

Greek peripoieomai (G4046) — to purchase, to acquire for oneself; “which he hath purchased with his own blood”, Acts 20:28.

Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend, to shepherd; “Feed the flock of God which is among you”, 1 Peter 5:2.

Hebrew raah (H7462) — to feed, to tend as a shepherd; “which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding”, Jeremiah 3:15.

Greek antechomai (G0472) — to hold fast, to cleave to; “Holding fast the faithful word”, Titus 1:9.

Usage

"“which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — what a congregation cost."

"“not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2) — the manner required of overseers."

"“Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9) — the qualification that cannot be waived."
